title: Petra and the Well
premise: Ansel Eastwick takes a teaching post in the hollow town of Marrowfen, where one student vanishes from each class every generation, and the town's founding families keep a well that 'sings back' whatever is lowered into it. Ansel, a nonbinary archivist fleeing a family that erased them, begins documenting the disappearances and discovers the missing children are not dead but held beneath the well by the Vessel—a thing fed by the town's founding bargain, sustained by a lullaby whose final verse was cut from every hymnal. With Petra Quill, the last heir of the founding family who has spent her life refusing her inheritance, Ansel learns that the well demands a keeper: someone must descend and stay, or the Vessel climbs out. In the end, Ansel and Petra refuse the binary of sacrifice or surrender—by teaching the town the whole song, verse and all, sung together, they dilute the Vessel's claim from one keeper to a chorus, freeing the children and binding the well to collective memory instead of a single body.
about_author: Theo Galloway is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent a decade cataloguing hymnals with pages razored out, and who has never confirmed which town inspired Marrowfen. They live above a flooded quarry with two cats and a standing rule against singing after dark.

chapters.title: The Position Is Vacant
chapters.summary: Ansel Eastwick arrives in Marrowfen by rain-soaked bus, hired to replace a teacher whose name the headmaster keeps forgetting. Ansel, whose family once struck them from the family Bible, finds comfort in meticulous notebooks. POV: Ansel. Beat: wary hope—the relief of being somewhere no one knows you, undercut by the town's too-smooth welcome.

chapters.title: Twenty-Six Desks
chapters.summary: Ansel's Year Seven class has twenty-six desks but twenty-five students, and no one will say who the extra desk was for. A girl named Wren Halloway whispers that the desk 'waits its turn.' Ansel photographs the classroom; the photo shows a faint shape at the empty desk. POV: Ansel. Beat: first dread—the documentation habit becomes a lifeline and a curse.

chapters.title: Petra of the Founding Families
chapters.summary: Ansel meets Petra Quill at the town's one pub, where she works but never drinks. She is the last Quill, heir to the deed on the well-house, and visibly flinches when the pub's clock strikes nine. She warns Ansel, kindly, to lock the school's music room. POV: Ansel. Beat: attraction sharpened by warning—Petra is duty's reluctant daughter.

chapters.title: The Song with a Hole in It
chapters.summary: Ansel finds the school hymnal's lullaby, 'The Well's Kind Keeping,' missing its final verse—razored out so cleanly the cut predates the printing. The music teacher, Mr. Sorrel, hums it perfectly but stops at the same bar every time, eyes wet. POV: Ansel. Beat: the shape of an absence; something was removed on purpose.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: At Petra's inherited cottage—where Ansel is lodging—the mirrors begin reflecting a beat behind. Ansel times it: exactly one second. Petra goes pale and says the house is 'listening for a Quill,' and Ansel's presence is confusing it. POV: Petra. Beat: intimacy under pressure; two people who chose to be invisible, seen by something else.

chapters.title: The Missing-Class Problem
chapters.summary: Ansel pulls fifty years of school registers: one child per class, every generation, always the quiet one, always 'transferred' with no forwarding school. The last was Wren's older brother, seven years ago. Ansel brings the file to the headmaster, who reads it and forgets it in front of them. POV: Ansel. Beat: institutional gaslighting; grief with a paper trail.

chapters.title: Wren Halloway's Map
chapters.summary: Wren, convinced Ansel will be next to notice, gives them a child's map of Marrowfen marked with places 'the hum is loud': the well-house, the church, the school's music room. The marks form a circle. Petra recognizes the pattern as the Quill property boundaries. POV: alternating Ansel and Wren. Beat: found family begins—an adult finally believes a child.

chapters.title: What the Well Sings Back
chapters.summary: Petra takes Ansel to the well-house at dusk and explains the founding bargain: the Quills fed it a keeper every generation, and it 'sang back' prosperity. Petra's mother refused, and the well has been hungry ever since—hence the missing children, taken as installments. POV: Petra. Beat: inheritance as horror; love against duty takes its first shape.

chapters.title: The Verse in Mother's Hand
chapters.summary: In the sealed Quill chapel, Petra finds her mother's hymnal—the final verse intact, in her mother's handwriting: a verse that gives the song an ending, and the ending is a name. Whoever is named in the singing belongs to the well. Petra's mother cut the verse from every copy to protect her. POV: Petra. Beat: a mother's terrible mercy; the inheritance is a sentence.

chapters.title: Reflections Out of Order
chapters.summary: The mirrors worsen: they show the room one second early now, showing what will happen. Ansel watches their reflection sit down before they do—and in the reflection, the classroom door is open, and something is standing in it. POV: Ansel. Beat: time running out made literal; documentation can't outrun prophecy.

chapters.title: The Town That Forgot on Purpose
chapters.summary: Ansel and Petra confront the town council, who admit everything in a flat, rehearsed way: forgetting is the payment's other half. Grief is rationed so the well stays fed. One elder, Mrs. Aldery, breaks rank and gives them her grandfather's account of the last full singing. POV: Ansel, with Petra. Beat: complicity revealed; the horror is communal, not monstrous.

chapters.title: Wren Hears Her Brother
chapters.summary: Wren follows the hum to the well-house alone and comes back changed—speaking a phrase of the lullaby she was never taught, in her brother's voice's cadence. The children below are learning the song from each other, and the well is teaching them the missing verse, wrong. POV: Wren. Beat: the stakes turn personal and urgent; the Vessel is corrupting the song.

chapters.title: Sorrel's Confession
chapters.summary: Mr. Sorrel admits he was the classmate who wasn't taken—chosen against, because the well wanted a Quill and got him instead. He has hummed the song for forty years as penance, keeping it alive but never complete. He gives Ansel his teacher's copy: the verse, and a warning that the Vessel has begun singing back up the well. POV: Sorrel. Beat: survivor's guilt; a mentor passes the burden.

chapters.title: The Well Chooses
chapters.summary: The well announces its choice: every mirror in town shows Ansel, not Petra, descending. The house's reflections now lead Ansel by a full minute. Petra realizes the Vessel prefers the erased—those with no family to sing their name back. Ansel's erasure made them the perfect keeper. POV: Petra. Beat: love against duty crystallizes; Petra will not let the town trade the unloved again.

chapters.title: What Petra's Mother Did
chapters.summary: Petra deciphers her mother's marginalia: her mother didn't just cut the verse—she sang a substitution, offering herself as a 'false keeper' to buy time, and the well has been slowly digesting her for years. Her voice is the hum Wren hears. Petra has been refusing an inheritance that was actually a hostage situation. POV: Petra. Beat: devastating reframe; the duty was never what she thought.

chapters.title: The Register of Names
chapters.summary: Ansel compiles the master document: every taken child, every generation, every name, cross-referenced with parish rolls. Documentation as prayer becomes literal—the ledger of names is a counter-song. Mrs. Aldery and Sorrel begin adding names from memory. POV: Ansel. Beat: quiet, fierce hope; the found family of the town's witnesses assembles.

chapters.title: The Night the Mirrors Stopped
chapters.summary: All reflections in Marrowfen go dark at once—the Vessel has finished learning the verse and no longer needs to watch. Wren doesn't come home. The town, finally unable to forget, wakes screaming with fifty years of returned grief. POV: alternating Ansel and Petra. Beat: the dam breaks; terror and terrible clarity.

chapters.title: Down the Singing Stair
chapters.summary: Ansel descends the well's inner stair to retrieve Wren, singing the ledger aloud as a shield of names, while Petra holds the well-house door against the Vessel's rising. Ansel finds the children—unaged, singing the corrupted verse in their mother's stolen voice. POV: Ansel. Beat: climax begins; sacrifice offered freely, but as a feint.

chapters.title: The Last Verse, Sung Wrong
chapters.summary: At the well's mouth, Petra begins the true final verse—naming herself, accepting the inheritance—and Ansel, from below, does the forbidden thing: sings along. Then Sorrel. Then Mrs. Aldery. Then the town, gathered at the well-house, every voice adding the name. A song meant for one keeper becomes a chorus no single throat owns. POV: Petra. Beat: climax; love against duty resolved by refusing the choice itself.

chapters.title: The Vessel Unmade
chapters.summary: The Vessel, built on the arithmetic of one name at a time, cannot parse a chorus—it thins into the water, and the well goes silent for the first time in three centuries. The children surface into the rain, Wren's brother seven years older and weeping. Petra's mother's voice, released, sings one clean note and stops. POV: Ansel. Beat: catharsis; the cost made visible, the debt discharged.

chapters.title: After the Silence
chapters.summary: Marlowfen—Marrowfen—begins the slow work of remembering: a memorial wall of the ledger's names, Sorrel teaching the whole song at last, Wren's family whole. Petra burns nothing and inherits everything, reframing the deed as stewardship. Ansel stays, hired properly, desk twenty-six retired with honors. POV: Ansel. Beat: found family settled; inheritance transformed into care.

chapters.title: The Room One Second Early
chapters.summary: A year later, Ansel's mirrors reflect on time—almost. Once, at dusk, the reflection lags a single heartbeat, and in it, something like a chorus of children waves. Ansel waves back, writes the date in the notebook, and leaves the porch light on for Petra. POV: Ansel. Beat: resolution with a held breath—some songs remember you back, and that's not always a threat.
